{{Short description|Identity relating to differential equations}}
{{redirect|Abel's formula|the formula on difference operators|Summation by parts}}
{{Differential equations|solution}}

In [[mathematics]], '''Abel's identity''' (also called '''Abel's formula'''<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/elementarydiffer00rain|url-access=registration|title=Elementary Differential Equations|last=Rainville|first=Earl David|last2=Bedient|first2=Phillip Edward|date=1969|publisher=Collier-Macmillan International Editions|language=en}}</ref> or '''Abel's differential equation identity''') is an equation that expresses the [[Wronskian]] of two solutions of a homogeneous second-order linear [[ordinary differential equation]] in terms of a coefficient of the original differential equation.
The relation can be generalised to ''n''th-order linear ordinary differential equations. The identity is named after the [[Norway|Norwegian]] [[mathematician]] [[Niels Henrik Abel]].

Since Abel's identity relates to the different [[linear independence|linearly independent]] solutions of the differential equation, it can be used to find one solution from the other. It provides useful identities relating the solutions, and is also useful as a part of other techniques such as the [[method of variation of parameters]]. It is especially useful for equations such as [[Bessel function|Bessel's equation]] where the solutions do not have a simple analytical form, because in such cases the Wronskian is difficult to compute directly.

A generalisation of first-order systems of homogeneous [[Linear differential equation|linear differential equations]] is given by [[Liouville's formula]].

==Statement==
Consider a [[Homogeneous differential equation|homogeneous]] linear second-order ordinary differential equation

: <math> y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)\,y = 0</math>

on an [[Interval (mathematics)|interval]] ''I'' of the [[real line]] with [[real number|real]]- or [[complex number|complex]]-valued [[continuous functions]] ''p'' and ''q''. Abel's identity states that the Wronskian <math>W=(y_1,y_2)</math> of two real- or complex-valued solutions <math>y_1</math> and <math>y_2</math> of this differential equation, that is the function defined by the [[determinant]]

: <math>W(y_1,y_2)(x)
=\begin{vmatrix}y_1(x)&y_2(x)\\y'_1(x)&y'_2(x)\end{vmatrix}
=y_1(x)\,y'_2(x) - y'_1(x)\,y_2(x),\quad x\in I,</math>

satisfies the relation

: <math>W(y_1,y_2)(x)=W(y_1,y_2)(x_0) \cdot \exp\left(-\int_{x_0}^x p(t) \,dt\right),\quad x\in I,</math>

for each point <math>x_0\in I</math>.

===Remarks===
* When the differential equation is real-valued, since <math>\exp\left(-\int_{x_0}^x p(t) \,dt\right)</math> is strictly positive, the Wronskian <math>W(y_1,y_2)</math> is always either identically zero, always positive, or always negative at every point <math>x</math> in <math>I</math>.
* If the two solutions <math>y_1</math> and <math>y_2</math> are linearly dependent, then the Wronskian is identically zero. Conversely, if the Wronskian is not zero at any point on the interval, then they are linearly independent.
* It is not necessary to assume that the second derivatives of the solutions <math>y_1</math> and <math>y_2</math> are continuous.
* If <math>p(x)=0</math> then <math>W</math> is constant.

===Proof===

{{Proof|title=|proof=

[[Derivative|Differentiating]] the Wronskian using the [[product rule]] gives (writing <math>W</math> for <math>W(y_1,y_2)</math> and omitting the argument <math>x</math> for brevity)

: <math>
\begin{align}
W' &= y_1' y_2' + y_1 y_2'' - y_1'' y_2 - y_1' y_2' \\
& = y_1 y_2'' - y_1'' y_2.
\end{align}
</math>

Solving for <math>y''</math> in the original differential equation yields

: <math> y'' = -(py'+qy). </math>

Substituting this result into the derivative of the Wronskian function to replace the second derivatives of <math>y_1</math> and <math>y_2</math> gives
: <math>
\begin{align}
 W'&= -y_1(py_2'+qy_2)+(py_1'+qy_1)y_2 \\
&= -p(y_1y_2'-y_1'y_2)\\
&= -pW.
\end{align}
</math>


Simplifying the equation to

: <math> W' + pW = 0 </math>

yields a homogeneous first order linear differential equation that can be solved by using the [[integrating factor]] <math>\exp\left(\int p(x)dx\right)</math> and [[Initial condition#Continuous_time|initial condition]] <math>W(x_0)</math>

: <math> W(x) = W(x_0) \cdot \exp\left(-\int_{x_0}^{x}{p(t)dt}\right) </math>

}}

==Generalization==
The Wronskian <math>W(y_1,\ldots,y_n)</math> of <math>n</math> functions <math>y_1,\ldots,y_n</math> on an interval <math>I</math> is the function defined by the determinant

: <math>W(y_1,\ldots,y_n)(x)
=\begin{vmatrix}
y_1(x) & y_2(x) & \cdots & y_n(x)\\
y'_1(x) & y'_2(x)& \cdots & y'_n(x)\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
y_1^{(n-1)}(x) & y_2^{(n-1)}(x) & \cdots & y_n^{(n-1)}(x)
\end{vmatrix},\qquad x\in I,</math>
Consider a homogeneous linear ordinary differential equation of order <math>n \geq 1</math>:

: <math>y^{(n)} + p_{n-1}(x)\,y^{(n-1)} + \cdots + p_1(x)\,y' + p_0(x)\,y = 0,</math>

on an interval <math>I</math> of the real line with a real- or complex-valued continuous function <math>p_{n-1}</math>. Let <math>y_1,\ldots,y_n</math> by solutions of this ''n''th order differential equation. Then the generalisation of Abel's identity states that this Wronskian satisfies the relation:

: <math>W(y_1,\ldots,y_n)(x)=W(y_1,\ldots,y_n)(x_0) \exp\biggl(-\int_{x_0}^x p_{n-1}(\xi) \,\textrm{d}\xi\biggr),\qquad x\in I,</math>

for each point <math>x_0\in I</math>.

===Direct proof===
For brevity, we write <math>W</math> for <math>W(y_1,\ldots,y_n)</math> and omit the argument <math>x</math>. It suffices to show that the Wronskian solves the first-order linear differential equation

:<math>W'=-p_{n-1}\,W,</math>

because the remaining part of the proof then coincides with the one for the case <math>n=2</math>.

In the case <math>n=1</math> we have <math>W=y_1</math> and the differential equation for <math>W</math> coincides with the one for <math>y_1</math>. Therefore, assume <math>n \geq 2</math> in the following.

The derivative of the Wronskian <math>W</math> is the derivative of the defining determinant. It follows from the [[Leibniz formula for determinants]] that this derivative can be calculated by differentiating every row separately, hence

: <math>\begin{align}W' & =
\begin{vmatrix}
y'_1 & y'_2 & \cdots & y'_n\\
y'_1 & y'_2 & \cdots & y'_n\\
y''_1 & y''_2 & \cdots & y''_n\\
y'''_1 & y'''_2 & \cdots & y'''_n\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
y_1^{(n-1)} & y_2^{(n-1)} & \cdots & y_n^{(n-1)}
\end{vmatrix}
+
\begin{vmatrix}
y_1 & y_2 & \cdots & y_n\\
y''_1 & y''_2 & \cdots & y''_n\\
y''_1 & y''_2 & \cdots & y''_n\\
y'''_1 & y'''_2 & \cdots & y'''_n\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
y_1^{(n-1)} & y_2^{(n-1)} & \cdots & y_n^{(n-1)}
\end{vmatrix}\\
&\qquad+\ \cdots\ +
\begin{vmatrix}
y_1 & y_2 & \cdots & y_n\\
y'_1 & y'_2 & \cdots & y'_n\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
y_1^{(n-3)} & y_2^{(n-3)} & \cdots & y_n^{(n-3)}\\
y_1^{(n-2)} & y_2^{(n-2)} & \cdots & y_n^{(n-2)}\\
y_1^{(n)} & y_2^{(n)} & \cdots & y_n^{(n)}
\end{vmatrix}.\end{align}
</math>

However, note that every determinant from the expansion contains a pair of identical rows, except the last one. Since determinants with linearly dependent rows are equal to 0, one is only left with the last one:

: <math>W'=
\begin{vmatrix}
y_1 & y_2 & \cdots & y_n\\
y'_1 & y'_2 & \cdots & y'_n\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
y_1^{(n-2)} & y_2^{(n-2)} & \cdots & y_n^{(n-2)}\\
y_1^{(n)} & y_2^{(n)} & \cdots & y_n^{(n)}
\end{vmatrix}.
</math>

Since every <math>y_i</math> solves the ordinary differential equation, we have

: <math>y_i^{(n)}  + p_{n-2}\,y_i^{(n-2)} + \cdots + p_1\,y'_i + p_0\,y_i = -p_{n-1}\,y_i^{(n-1)}</math>

for every <math>i \in \lbrace 1,\ldots,n \rbrace</math>. Hence, adding to the last row of the above determinant <math>p_0</math> times its first row, <math>p_1</math> times its second row, and so on until <math>p_{n-2}</math> times its next to last row, the value of the determinant for the derivative of <math>W</math> is unchanged and we get

: <math>W'=
\begin{vmatrix}
y_1 & y_2 & \cdots & y_n \\
y'_1 & y'_2 & \cdots & y'_n \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
y_1^{(n-2)} & y_2^{(n-2)} & \cdots & y_n^{(n-2)} \\
-p_{n-1}\,y_1^{(n-1)} & -p_{n-1}\,y_2^{(n-1)} & \cdots & -p_{n-1}\,y_n^{(n-1)}
\end{vmatrix}
=-p_{n-1}W.
</math>

===Proof using Liouville's formula===
The solutions <math>y_1,\ldots,y_n</math> form the square-matrix valued solution

:<math>\Phi(x)=\begin{pmatrix}
y_1(x) & y_2(x) & \cdots & y_n(x)\\
y'_1(x) & y'_2(x)& \cdots & y'_n(x)\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
y_1^{(n-2)}(x) & y_2^{(n-2)}(x) & \cdots & y_n^{(n-2)}(x)\\
y_1^{(n-1)}(x) & y_2^{(n-1)}(x) & \cdots & y_n^{(n-1)}(x)
\end{pmatrix},\qquad x\in I,</math>

of the <math>n</math>-dimensional first-order system of homogeneous linear differential equations

:<math>\begin{pmatrix}y'\\y''\\\vdots\\y^{(n-1)}\\y^{(n)}\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0&\cdots&0\\
0&0&1&\cdots&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
0&0&0&\cdots&1\\
-p_0(x)&-p_1(x)&-p_2(x)&\cdots&-p_{n-1}(x)\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}y\\y'\\\vdots\\y^{(n-2)}\\y^{(n-1)}\end{pmatrix}.</math>

The [[trace (linear algebra)|trace]] of this matrix is <math>-p_{n-1}(x)</math>, hence Abel's identity follows directly from [[Liouville's formula]].
